newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK PSBR to ease on privatisation proceeds.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK PSBR to ease on privatisation proceeds.

text.p: Privatisation proceeds of around one billion stg are expected to reduce the UK September budget deficit substantially from the 4.5 billion stg reported in August. September data are due at 0830 GMT on Wednesday.
The Reuters consensus forecast is for a September public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) of around 2.7 billion stg but some forecasters see a much lower figure.

"The fiscal deficit is likely to fall quite sharply from a year ago in September because of high privatisation proceeds," said Michael Saunders of Salomon Brothers, who predicts a shortfall of 2.1 billion stg.

Receipts from the privatisation of power companies should bring in around one billion stg. The deficit excluding privatisation should dip only slightly to 3.1 billion stg from 3.3 billion a year earlier, he said.

"The deficit is likely to fall more rapidly in the latter half of the fiscal year because of base effects from the echo of high spending figures in the latter half of the 1995/96 fiscal year," Saunders said, adding that local authority borrowing should also fall back.
Goldman Sachs chief economist Gavyn Davies, one of the Treasury's independent advisers, sees economic growth boosting revenue for the rest of the year.

"Recent monthly figures for the PSBR have been very volatile, but the intense rise in consumer spending should fill the Treasury coffers from now on," he wrote in Monday's Independent newspaper. Philip Shaw of Union Discount said neither receipts nor spending have followed the same seasonal pattern as in previous years recently, making it difficult to discern the true underlying trend.
He forecasts a 2.0 billion stg budget deficit in September but his full-year PSBR forecast of 28 billion stg is slightly above the Treasury's latest estimate of 27 billion.
"Despite a likely pickup in economic activity over the remainder of the period, we do not envisage a significant undershoot of this total," Shaw said.

Analysts at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell expect a September deficit of 2.1 billion stg. "This month we expect some rebound and further evidence of control of public spending," they wrote in a client note.

Economists at HSBC Markets say the spending side presents the greatest threat to the public finances this year, but noted that receipts growth was holding up well. They see a September PSBR shortfall of 2.5 billion stg.
